newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi economy keeping pace - annual report.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi economy keeping pace - annual report.

text.p: Mississippi's economy is keeping pace with the rest of the nation, with a slowdown in manufacturing offset by growth in services, the state said in its annual report for fiscal 1996, which ended June 30.
Overall employment grew at a modest 0.6 percent in 1996, but two sectors, construction and amusements ad gaming, grew by an impressive 10 percent.

"Construction spending continues strong, with building permits issued year-to-date indicating that this trend will continue well into 1997," Edward Ranck, executive director of the state Department of Finance and Administration, wrote in the report.
Gaming revenues increased by about $15.8 million from fiscal 1995 to fiscal 1996.

Gross state product was projected to rise by 0.5 percent in 1997, compared to an estimated 4.8 percent in 1996, while personal income growth was expected to remain steady at 5 percent annually in 1997 and 1998.
Since 1982, companies have invested more than $8 billioin in new and expanded industries in the state.
"The state of Mississippi has a firm grounding in five years of consistent economic growth," the report said.
Total revenues increased by $234 million in fiscal 1996, to $7.07 billioin, with 91 percent of the increase due to rising collections of sales and use taxes and income taxes.
Revenues from gaming fees, licenses and permits increased by $15.88 million, or 12 percent, to $148 million. Gaming also contributed to the growth in sales taxes, the report said.
The overall revenue increase came despite a $42 million drop Medicaid revenues, the report said.

Expenditures increased by 12.5 percernt, to $6.76 billion. Debt service expenditures decreased by $87 million in fiscal 1996 as a result of the defeasance of limited obligation bonds in 1995, the report said.
The state issued $288.7 million of general obligation bonds in fiscal 1996, putting total GO bonds outstanding $1.2 bilion as of June 30.
Total bond indebtedness comprised only 20 percent of the $6 billion ceiling set by the legislature, the report said.
